opening.spoken: This record covers the claimed solution of Erdős problem #671: what has been claimed, what it rests on, and what would have to be checked by whom.

short_version.spoken: Erdős asked whether a sequence of interpolation nodes can make the Lebesgue function blow up at a point, or everywhere, while Lagrange interpolation still converges somewhere for every continuous function. Two claimed solutions were listed in July 2026, both answering yes to both questions, both produced with AI systems and both with a Lean file. Nobody independent has reported building either Lean file or reading either argument. Everything here is open.

what_happened.spoken: The claim was pinned from the public record: the problem page, the proof-claims thread, and every artifact the claimants made public, by commit or hash. Nervous Machine then wrote a reading guide that lays the Lean statement beside the problem page, definition by definition. Doing so it found that the first claim's listed Lean link is cut off at 2048 characters, recovered the full link from the claimant's own comments, decoded it offline and pinned the text by hash, and found that the second claim's Lean file is the first with changes inside the proofs only, so both claims state the same theorem. Nothing was built or run. The gaps that follow are the checks still owed.

cycles.spoken: Terence Tao's Erdős-problems AI wiki listed an AI-standalone candidate full solution with Lean for problem 671, dated June 22, 2026, marked unverified; the wiki stopped updating on June 30. Liam Price listed a proof claim on the problem page: both questions answered in the affirmative by GPT Pro, with a Lean formalisation by GPT-5.5 in Codex. QuietMethod listed a second proof claim, described as an independent re-derivation and refinement of the first, with a Lean file and a PDF write-up; this record pins both files by hash as fetched on November 14, 2026. The problem page lists two proof claims, neither marked accepted by the site, and no third-party formalisation of the problem statement.

cycles.spoken: Nervous Machine wrote the reading guide for the one question on this record that a machine cannot settle: whether the Lean statement of problem 671 says what Erdős asked. There is no third-party formal statement, so the guide lays the claimants' own statement beside the problem page. On the way it recovered the first claimant's full Lean text: the link listed on the problem page is cut off at 2048 characters, but the full link is in the claimant's own comments, and decoding it offline gives a file now pinned by hash. That file and the second claimant's file state the same theorem with the same definitions; the second is the first with changes inside the proofs, as its author's page says. The guide traces every symbol to Mathlib with file and line and records ten conventions, none of which changes the meaning in the agent's reading. Seven worked examples are written for Lean but have not been run. The readings are the system's, not a mathematician's, so nothing changed standing. An analyst can now sign or refuse four lines in under an hour.

background.spoken: For each n take n nodes in [-1,1] and interpolate a continuous function f by the polynomial of degree n-1 that agrees with f at those nodes. The Lebesgue function at a point x is the sum of the absolute values of the fundamental polynomials at x; Bernstein showed it is unbounded at some point for every choice of nodes. Erdős asked two things. First: can the nodes be chosen so that for every continuous f there is a point where the Lebesgue function is unbounded and yet the interpolants converge to f? Second: can the nodes be chosen so that the Lebesgue function is unbounded at every point, and yet for every continuous f the interpolants converge to f somewhere?

background.spoken: A second claim, described by its author as an independent re-derivation and quantitative refinement of the first, not claiming priority for the construction. It builds nested intervals of nodes so that the Lebesgue function exceeds any bound everywhere, while a pigeonhole choice at each stage keeps the interpolation error small for a given f. The author reports a Lean formalisation checked with Lean 4.33.0-rc1 and Mathlib, with no sorry or admit, and with the axioms reported as propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.
